plan.contextChunk:
One classical example of the limitations of motion estimation from
images is the **aperture problem**. The aperture problem happens when
observing the motion of a one-dimensional (1D) structure larger than the
image frame, as shown in @fig-apperture_problem. If none of the
termination points are in view within the observation window (i.e., the
aperture), it is impossible to measure the actual image motion. Only the
component orthogonal to the moving structure can be measured.

![Aperture problem when observing the motion of a one-dimensional (1D) structure larger than the image frame. The actual motion of the bar is upward, but the perception, when vision is limited to what is visible within the observation window, appears as if the motion of the bar is in the direction perpendicular to the bar.](figures/optical_flow/apperture_problem.png){width="100%" #fig-apperture_problem}


:::{.column-margin}
The **Barber-pole illusion** is an illustration of the aperture problem. The barber pole induces the illusion of downward motion while rotating.

![](figures/optical_flow/barber_pole.png){width="40%"}
:::


### Representation of Optical Flow

We can model motion over time as a sequence of **dense optical flow**
images: $$\left[ u(x,y,t), v(x,y,t) \right]$$ The quantities $u(x,y,t)$and $v(x,y,t)$ indicate that a pixel at image coordinates $(x,y)$ at
time $t$ moves with velocity $(u,v)$. The problem with this formulation
is that we do not have an explicit representation of the trajectory
followed by points in the scene over time. As time $t$ changes, the
location $(x,y)$ might correspond to different scene elements.

An alternative representation is to model motion as a **sparse set of
moving points** (tracks):
$$\left\{ \mathbf{P}^{(i)}_t \right\}_{i=1}^N$$ This has the challenge

elements: vertical cylinder with a helical red, white, and blue spiral stripe pattern
top circular cap of the cylinder, visible due to the elevated perspective
bottom circular cap of the cylinder
curved 3D arrow floating above the cylinder indicating 'Real motion' (horizontal rotation)
vertical 3D arrow pointing downwards next to the cylinder indicating 'Observed motion'
text labels for 'Real motion' and 'Observed motion' aligned with their respective arrows
optional local measurement point on a stripe boundary
aperture mask: a flat square card with a circular hole placed directly in front of the cylinder's surface
motion vector indicators: actual horizontal velocity vector (tangent), perpendicular/normal velocity vector (perpendicular to stripe), and illusory vertical velocity vector

interactions.label: Rotation Speed
interactions.teaches: Adjusting the cylinder's physical rotation speed changes both the actual angular velocity and the speed of the perceived downward/upward vertical illusion.

interactions.label: Aperture View
interactions.teaches: Placing a small circular aperture over the pattern isolates a single line segment, making horizontal rotation completely invisible and leaving only the perpendicular motion visible.

demo_steps.title: The Barber-pole Illusion
demo_steps.narration: Observe the rotating cylinder. Although the physical motion is purely horizontal (Real motion, rotating around the vertical axis), the stripes appear to continuously slide downwards (Observed motion). This is a classic visual illusion caused by how our brains interpret moving edges.

demo_steps.title: The Aperture Problem
demo_steps.narration: Toggle the aperture view. By looking through a small circular window, we can no longer see the cylinder's boundaries. Because the stripe is a 1D line, any motion parallel to it is invisible; we can only detect motion perpendicular to the stripe edge. This ambiguity is the fundamental aperture problem in optical flow.

demo_steps.title: Reversing the physical rotation
demo_steps.narration: Reverse the cylinder's rotation direction. Notice how the stripes inside the aperture now appear to glide in the opposite perpendicular direction, and the full barber pole illusion reverses to show upward motion. The visual system resolves the aperture ambiguity consistently based on rotation direction.

demo_steps.title: How boundaries resolve ambiguity
demo_steps.narration: Remove the aperture. Why does the full pole look vertical rather than diagonal? The long vertical edges of the cylinder act as 'terminator' boundaries. The motion of stripe endpoints along these vertical edges strongly signals vertical motion, which our visual system propagates to dominate the entire pattern.

interactionPlan.camera_suggestion: Slightly elevated front-on orthographic view showing the top cap of the cylinder clearly and framing the full vertical length of the pole.
interactionPlan.view_reasoning: (1) The dominant vertical axis of the cylinder runs straight up-down on the screen. (2) The circular top of the cylinder is projected as a highly foreshortened ellipse, showing that the camera is positioned broadside to the vertical axis (azimuth 0) but looking slightly down. (3) The flat, highly compressed shape of the top cap ellipse indicates a shallow elevation angle of approximately 15 degrees, with no roll.

camera_view.view_notes: The orthographic projection preserves the straight vertical lines of the cylinder walls. The elevation of 15 degrees matches the visible perspective of the top cap ellipse.

inline_constraints.default_view: Must closely match the original silhouette, stripe spacing, and placement of label text and arrows.
inline_constraints.visible_ui: At most 2 compact controls (rotation speed slider and aperture toggle) placed unobtrusively near the bottom or top edge without a background panel.
inline_constraints.explainers: Tooltip overlays only, explaining vector directions when hovered.
inline_constraints.framing: Maintain vertical whitespace around the cylinder to ensure the 'Real motion' arrow has sufficient clearance at the top.
inline_constraints.camera: Match the visual style of the static textbook figure as a direct 3D upgrade.

interactionPlan.notes: Create the helical stripe pattern using a custom shader or a mapped canvas texture with diagonal red, white, and blue stripes. The rotation animation must continuously update the texture offset or rotate the cylinder geometry around the Y-axis. The aperture mask should be rendered as a flat plane with a transparent circular hole in the center, positioned slightly in front of the cylinder to avoid z-fighting.

evaluation.geometry_accuracy_analysis: The 3D geometry accurately reconstructs the source figure. The barber pole is built from a CylinderGeometry with custom procedural shader stripes, closed with caps and outlined with silhouette lines. The real motion indicator is a 3D curved tube, and the observed motion is a vertical ArrowHelper. Spatial relationships, scale, and the orthographic camera angle match the original almost perfectly, including the elliptical projection of the top cap.
evaluation.geometry_accuracy_improvement: Adjust the curved tube geometry of the 'Real motion' arrow to have a wider horizontal span, matching the flatter, wider oval trajectory in the source figure.
evaluation.interactivity_usability_analysis: The developer built three robust, functional interactions: (1) A 'Rotation Speed' slider that dynamically adjusts the shader phase velocity and physical rotation direction, (2) An 'Aperture View' toggle that overlays an aperture mask and exposes local measurement vectors, and (3) An interactive step-through guided demonstration (4 steps with narration and smooth parameter tweening) triggered by clicking interactive objects (the pole or aperture mask) in the scene. Additionally, rich descriptive tooltips/hover details are implemented via registerInteractive on all key visual elements.

Proportions are slightly wider, and the curved motion indicator on top is thicker with a spherical cap instead of a sharp 2D arrowhead.
discrepancies: Cylinder aspect ratio is slightly shorter and wider than the original
The rotational arrow on top has a round bulbous end instead of a sharp arrowhead
Added interactive UI elements at the bottom left
evaluation.faithfulness_improvement: Refine the top rotational arrow geometry to use a flat, sharp arrowhead pointing to the right to match the clean 2D schematic look of the original.
evaluation.label_quality_analysis: Source labels: 'Real motion' and 'Observed motion'. Both labels feature accurate text and clean layout matching the original figure.
evaluation.label_quality_improvement: Refine the curved arrow geometry under 'Real motion' to have a clean, sharp arrowhead instead of a round cap.
evaluation.concept_accuracy_analysis: Core concept: The Barber-pole illusion and the Aperture problem. The interactive figure accurately demonstrates that a cylinder rotating horizontally (real motion) produces an illusory vertical motion (observed motion) due to the slanted 1D stripe edges. User-visible claims: (1) "Real motion" (curved horizontal arrow) vs "Observed motion" (vertical arrow) - highly accurate. (3) Local velocity vectors (tangent, normal, and perceived) are accurately oriented and dynamically flip when rotation direction is reversed.
evaluation.notes: The interactive figure captures the barber-pole illusion beautifully with highly accurate physical logic, excellent guided steps, and clear visual labels. interactionPlan.notes: Create the helical stripe pattern using a custom shader or a mapped canvas texture with diagonal red, white, and blue stripes. The rotation animation must continuously update the texture offset or rotate the cylinder geometry around the Y-axis. The aperture mask should be rendered as a flat plane with a transparent circular hole in the center, positioned slightly in front of the cylinder to avoid z-fighting.

evaluation.geometry_accuracy_analysis: The 3D geometry of the barber pole cylinder, including its helical striping pattern, circular caps, and black outlines, is accurately reconstructed using real 3D primitives (CylinderGeometry, TubeGeometry, and custom ShaderMaterial). The 'Real motion' curved arrow and 'Observed motion' straight arrow are also correctly constructed and positioned in 3D space to match the reference layout. Viewpoint and proportions are highly consistent with the source image.
evaluation.geometry_accuracy_improvement: Slightly adjust the vertical positioning of the 'Real motion' label and curved arrow to reduce overlapping and match the spacing of the source image more closely.
evaluation.interactivity_usability_analysis: The developer implemented multiple highly functional and pedagogically useful interactions: (1) A 'Rotation Speed' slider that dynamically controls the cylinder's shader-based rotation speed and direction (including reversing it); (2) An 'Aperture View' toggle that masks the cylinder, revealing the aperture problem and displaying three distinct velocity vector arrows (actual, normal, and illusion); (3) A fully functional guided step-through system integrated into the scene, where clicking on interactive objects (like the pole or aperture card) advances the narrative steps, updating both the scene state and presenting explanatory popup content; (4) Multiple rich hover-tooltips via `registerInteractive` that explain the physics of each visual element (real motion arrow, observed motion arrow, measurement points, etc.).
evaluation.faithfulness_analysis: The rendered output is highly faithful to the source image, capturing the exact barber pole design, color schemes, and annotations. The text layout, arrow directions, and pole geometry are instantly recognizable and match the diagram's composition well. Minor issues include slight overlap between the top text and its corresponding curved arrow, and the presence of UI elements in the lower-left corner.
discrepancies: Slight overlap between the 'Real motion' text and the rotation arrow
Extra interactive UI elements (Rotation Speed slider and Aperture View checkbox) not present in the original diagram
The downward arrow style is thinner than the blocky arrow in the reference
evaluation.faithfulness_improvement: Adjust the vertical spacing of the 'Real motion' label upward to prevent overlapping with the curved rotation arrow.
evaluation.label_quality_analysis: Source labels: 'Real motion' and 'Observed motion'. Output captures both with appropriate serif styling. However, 'Real motion' slightly overlaps the rotating arrow geometry, causing minor legibility issues.
evaluation.label_quality_improvement: Increase the vertical offset of the 'Real motion' label to position it completely above the curved arrow indicator.
evaluation.concept_accuracy_analysis: The figure illustrates the barber-pole illusion and the aperture problem. All concepts are represented with extremely high accuracy: (1) 'Real motion' correctly shows the physical rotation around the vertical axis; (2) 'Observed motion' correctly shows the illusory vertical movement; (3) The 'Aperture View' isolates a single stripe segment, illustrating how the lack of boundary cues restricts observable motion to the perpendicular vector (cyan); (4) The step narration correctly explains how the vertical boundaries (terminators) resolve the ambiguity of the 1D stripes to create a vertical illusion. The vector math for tangent, normal, and vertical components is physically and perceptually sound.
evaluation.notes: The figure is excellent, featuring a highly accurate 3D barber-pole shader, fully functional aperture simulations, and clear interactive steps. The only minor issues are visual overlaps near the top and the styling of the observed motion arrow.
